title: A comparison of British and German parliamentary discourses on science diplomacy over time
method: Comparative qualitative content analysis of parliamentary discourse.
materials: 72 parliamentary speeches concerning science and Russia from the German Bundestag and British House of Commons, February 2014–December 2022.
question: How do MPs of different political parties discuss science diplomacy over time, how do British and German parliamentary debates differ, and how do views change in relation to Russia?
relation: Useful model for a document-only design focused on discourse over time. Could inspire periodisation of Chinese policy documents and comparison of how international scientific cooperation is framed across phases.
notes: Potential template if the thesis becomes primarily about how official understandings of international scientific cooperation change over time.

authors: Michał Łuszczuk, Barbora Padrtová & Natalia Szczerbowicz
title: Political dimension of Arctic research
method: Quantitative and qualitative discourse/content analysis; qualitative predicate analysis combined with text-frequency analysis.
materials: National Arctic policy documents and Arctic research strategies from 17 European states.
question: What rationales do states give for Arctic research, and how are scientific and political dimensions of research related in national policy?
relation: Very close to the simple substantive question: what is the relationship between scientific and political/diplomatic goals? Shows that this can be studied directly from official documents without presupposing that science is merely a foreign-policy instrument.
notes: Especially useful if I want to distinguish scientific rationales from political/diplomatic rationales in Science Silk Road documents.

title: Science diplomacy as a foreign policy tool for Turkey and the ramifications of collaboration with the EU
method: Qualitative content analysis and policy-process reconstruction using public documentary sources.
materials: Policy reports, policy papers, EU communications, directives, press releases, speeches, World Bank/OECD reports, scholarly literature and digital documents.
question: How can science diplomacy help explain Turkey’s changing STI policy and its scientific and political relationship with European research programmes?
relation: Useful for source triangulation: one project can be reconstructed from government documents, partner-side materials, reports, press releases and institutional webpages. Less useful as a purely sociological theory template.
notes: Good source-collection template for projects where no single authoritative document gives the whole story.

title: The Science Policy Script, Revised
method: Historical/institutional case analysis based on documentary evidence, interpreted through a postcolonial STS perspective.
materials: Swiss international science-policy instruments and measures, administrative arrangements, policy classifications, official decisions and related documentary materials.
question: What happens to established science-policy categories when emerging and developing countries are incorporated into international science policy, and how does this challenge the distinction between scientific cooperation and development cooperation?
relation: Most useful for treating institutional arrangements as sociological evidence. Variables such as category, funding, lead institution, administrative ownership, access and evaluation criteria are not just background—they can reveal how cooperation is institutionally organised and classified.
notes: Important theoretical/methodological bridge from my structured project dataset to a sociological argument.

title: Between global collaboration and national competition: Unraveling the many faces of Arctic science diplomacy
method: Qualitative content analysis plus comparative case studies; combines a top-down strategy analysis with bottom-up reconstruction of concrete science-diplomacy cases.
materials: Arctic strategies plus two concrete cases: the Agreement on Enhancing International Arctic Scientific Cooperation and research activities on Svalbard; documentary and legal materials are central.
question: How do collaboration and competition coexist in Arctic science diplomacy, and what different forms of science-diplomacy activity can be identified?
relation: Probably the closest structural template for this thesis: combine top-down policy documents with bottom-up comparison of concrete Science Silk Road projects. Could compare joint labs, science parks, big-science infrastructure, technology-transfer centres and training programmes against official policy narratives.
notes: Strong candidate for overall research-design model: policy layer + project layer.
